name: Sakya
alt_names: the school of the 'Grey Earth' (sa skya) monastery
regions: Kham and Amdo (Derge Gönchen, Lhundrub Teng)

tradition.text: Lamdre revealed to Virūpa by the goddess Nairātmyā; brought to Tibet by Gayadhara and Drokmi; Sakya monastery founded by Khön Könchok Gyalpo 1073

scholarly.text: Sakya monastery 1073 CE; the school's identity fixed by the 'five founding masters' (1092–1280 CE); Sakya–Yuan hegemony over Tibet c. 1260–1354

transmissions_received.what: the Path with its Result (Lamdre) of Virūpa and the Hevajra cycle; the 'eight later cycles of the path' (lam skor phyi ma brgyad)
transmissions_received.evidence: Sakya lineage lists (Virūpa → Kāṇha → Ḍamarupa → Avadhūtipa → Gayadhara → Drokmi); Vajra Verses Tōh 2284 in the Tengyur

transmissions_received.what: the Khön family's inherited Vajrakīlaya and Yangdak Heruka practice
Dharmakīrti's epistemology as read in Sakya Paṇḍita's Treasury of Reasoning
mind training and the Mahāyāna gradual path (Parting from the Four Attachments commentaries; Tokmé Zangpo)
Candrakīrti's Madhyamaka read as freedom from elaborations (spros bral)

transmissions_given.what: Tsongkhapa's Madhyamaka and early training under the Sakya master Rendawa; many tantric lineages
Ngor and Tshar Lamdre and the Sakya collections re-transmitted by Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Jamgön Kongtrul

distinctive_positions: The Path with its Result (lam 'bras): the result is already present in the cause, so path and result are taught together; the whole path is laid out as the three visions (impure, experiential, pure) and the three continua (causal/all-base, method/body, result/Mahāmudrā).
View of the inseparability of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa ('khor 'das dbyer med), the union of clarity and emptiness of the all-base causal continuum.
Parting from the Four Attachments (zhen pa bzhi bral), received by Sachen Kunga Nyingpo from Mañjuśrī, as the summary of the whole common path.
Sakya Paṇḍita's insistence that Mahāmudrā is the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages; his critique of a self-sufficient 'white panacea' Mahāmudrā as Chinese-style (Hwashang) teaching.
Three vows (prātimokṣa, bodhisattva, tantric) must be kept distinct and each by its own rules (Discrimination of the Three Vows).
Madhyamaka (Gorampa): the final view is freedom from all four extremes (spros bral), not a mere negation of inherent existence; Tsongkhapa's reading rejected as 'nihilist Madhyamaka'.
Epistemology (Sakya Paṇḍita): universals are conceptual constructions, not real entities, against the earlier Sangphu realists.
Leadership of the school by the Khön family (Sakya Trizin), with the Ngor, Tshar and Dzong sub-schools.
summary: The Sakya school, centred on the Khön family's monastery of Sakya (1073) and its 'five founding masters', transmits Virūpa's Path with its Result (Lamdre) with the Hevajra tantra as its core, the mind-training summary Parting from the Four Attachments, and a strong scholastic tradition (Sakya Paṇḍita's epistemology and Three Vows; Gorampa's and Shākya Chokden's Madhyamaka).

name: Ngor (Ngorpa) Sakya
distinctive_positions: Holds the Sakya Path with its Result and the Khön family's teaching lineages; distinguished from the other Sakya lines by its own transmission and monastic seat.
summary: Sub-school founded by Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo at Ngor Evaṃ Chöden (1429), keeper of the Lamdre Lobshé ('explanation for disciples') and of strict monastic discipline; famed for its mandala rituals and Vajrayoginī and Hevajra transmissions.

name: Tshar (Tsharpa) Sakya
distinctive_positions: Holds the Sakya Path with its Result and the Khön family's teaching lineages; distinguished from the other Sakya lines by its own transmission and monastic seat.
summary: Sub-school stemming from Tsarchen Losal Gyatso (1502–1566), who re-transmitted the Lamdre Lobshé as a hidden oral instruction and the 'thirteen golden dharmas'; associated with Nalendra monastery.

name: Dzong (Dzongpa) Sakya
distinctive_positions: Holds the Sakya Path with its Result and the Khön family's teaching lineages; distinguished from the other Sakya lines by its own transmission and monastic seat.
summary: Sub-school from Dzongpa Kunga Namgyal (1432–1496) at Gongkar Dorjeden, known for its own transmission lines of Sakya tantric instructions; small and largely absorbed today.

name: Kadam
alt_names: 'those who take all the Buddha's words (bka') as personal instruction (gdams)'
the Old Kadam (as distinct from the Gelug 'New Kadam')

tradition.text: Atiśa invited to Tibet by the Ngari kings Yeshe Ö and Jangchub Ö; Reting founded by Dromtönpa after Atiśa's death

scholarly.text: Atiśa in Tibet 1042–1054 CE; Reting 1056/57; Kadam as a separate order absorbed into the Gelug from the 15th c. and its lojong and lamrim into all schools

transmissions_received.what: the two bodhicitta lineages — 'profound view' (Nāgārjuna) and 'vast conduct' (Asaṅga) — and the mind-training of exchanging self and other from Serlingpa, Dharmarakṣita and Maitrīyogin
Candrakīrti as the one who realized emptiness (Satyadvayāvatāra 15)
Atiśa's tantric transmissions (Guhyasamāja, the four deities practice)

transmissions_given.what: the lamrim structure of the three scopes, the four deities and six texts, and lojong ('New Kadam')
the Kadam gradual path joined by Gampopa with Mahāmudrā ('the two streams of Kadam and Mahāmudrā')
mind training, taught by Sakya masters such as Tokmé Zangpo

distinctive_positions: All the Buddha's words are to be taken as personal instruction for practice; none is to be discarded as irrelevant.
The path is graded for three kinds of person (small, middling, great) — Bodhipathapradīpa 2–5.
Mind training (blo sbyong): relative bodhicitta by equalizing and exchanging self and other, sending and taking; turning adversity into the path.
The seven divine dharmas (lha chos bdun ldan): the four deities (Śākyamuni, Avalokiteśvara, Tārā, Acala) and the three baskets.
The six Kadam treatises (bka' gdams gzhung drug) as core texts.
Celibate monastics are not to take the secret and wisdom initiations literally (Bodhipathapradīpa 66–68).
Madhyamaka in Candrakīrti's line: the ultimate is one, not realized by the two means of valid cognition taken as conceptual (Satyadvayāvatāra 4, 10).
summary: The Kadam, founded on Atiśa's teaching in Tibet (1042–1054) and organised by his lay disciple Dromtönpa at Reting, stressed renunciation, bodhicitta and the graded path for three persons (Lamp for the Path), and produced the mind-training (lojong) literature — Langri Tangpa's Eight Verses, Chekawa's Seven Points — that all later schools adopted; its lines were absorbed into the Gelug ('New Kadam').

name: Kadam Shungpawa (textual tradition)
distinctive_positions: One of the three Kadam transmission lines distinguished by Tibetan historians (textual, lamrim, oral-instruction).
summary: The Kadam line that trained through study of the six Kadam treatises, traced to Potowa Rinchen Sal.
notes: The assignment of founders to the three lines differs between Tibetan histories; recalled, not checked.

name: Kadam Lamrimpa (stages-of-the-path tradition)
distinctive_positions: One of the three Kadam transmission lines distinguished by Tibetan historians (textual, lamrim, oral-instruction).
summary: The Kadam line that transmitted the graded path (lamrim) as a meditation sequence; traced by Tibetan historians to Gönpawa and Neusurpa. Tsongkhapa received it through Lhodrak Namkha Gyaltsen and others.
notes: The assignment of founders to the three lines differs between Tibetan histories; recalled, not checked.

name: Kadam Mengakpa (oral-instruction tradition)
distinctive_positions: One of the three Kadam transmission lines distinguished by Tibetan historians (textual, lamrim, oral-instruction).
summary: The Kadam line that transmitted the pith instructions (including the sixteen-drop practice of the Book of Kadam), traced to Chengawa Tsultrim Bar.
notes: The assignment of founders to the three lines differs between Tibetan histories; recalled, not checked.

name: Gelug
alt_names: the New Kadam (bka' gdams gsar ma)
the Yellow Hats (name used by others)
regions: diaspora (South India re-foundations of the great monasteries)

tradition.text: founded by Tsongkhapa, regarded as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, at Ganden in 1409; the tradition counts it as the renewal of Atiśa's Kadam

scholarly.text: Ganden 1409 CE; ruling school of the Ganden Phodrang government from 1642 CE

transmissions_received.what: lamrim, lojong, the Kadam deities and texts (hence 'New Kadam')
transmissions_received.evidence: Lamrim Chenmo builds on the Bodhipathapradīpa

transmissions_received.what: Candrakīrti's Prāsaṅgika as the final view
transmissions_received.evidence: Lamrim Chenmo insight section; Illumination of the Thought

transmissions_received.what: Tsongkhapa's training under Rendawa; many tantric lines
Dharmakīrti's epistemology via the Sangphu and Sakya traditions
the Guhyasamāja of the Ārya tradition as the king of tantras

transmissions_given.what: Gelug texts studied in Rimé curricula (as an influence, not a lineage merger)

distinctive_positions: The three principal aspects of the path — renunciation, bodhicitta and the correct view — frame the whole of sūtra and tantra.
Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka as the final view: the object of negation is inherent existence (existence from the object's own side), to be identified precisely — neither too broadly nor too narrowly.
Emptiness is a non-affirming negation; it is fully compatible with conventionally valid cause and effect (dependent arising), and ultimate truth is an object of knowledge.

Tsongkhapa's 'eight difficult points' distinguishing Prāsaṅgika (no ālaya distinct from the six consciousnesses; no reflexive awareness; no autonomous syllogisms; external objects conventionally accepted; śrāvakas realize the selflessness of phenomena; grasping at the self of phenomena is an affliction; disintegration is a functioning thing; the special account of the three times).
Analytical meditation is indispensable, not an obstacle to non-conceptual realization; insight arises when analysis itself induces pliancy.
Tantra is distinguished from sūtra by deity yoga (method), not by a higher view; strict monastic discipline is kept alongside Highest Yoga Tantra (Guhyasamāja, Cakrasaṃvara, Vajrabhairava).
Monastic education through debate on the five great texts, leading to the geshe degree.
summary: The Gelug school, founded by Tsongkhapa Lobsang Drakpa (1357–1419) at Ganden and continued by his disciples Gyaltsab Je and Khedrup Je and the great monasteries of Drepung, Sera and Tashi Lhunpo, unites the Kadam graded path with Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka and the Highest Yoga Tantras under strict monastic discipline; its lines of Dalai and Panchen Lamas and its debate curriculum made it the largest Tibetan school.

name: Ganden Oral Lineage of Mahāmudrā (Ganden Kagyu / Ensa Hearing Lineage)
alt_names: dben sa snyan brgyud (Ensa Hearing Lineage)

tradition.text: Mahāmudrā received by Tsongkhapa from Mañjuśrī and passed orally until the First Panchen Lama wrote it down

scholarly.text: oral lineage claimed from the 15th c.; root text written c. early 17th c. CE

distinctive_positions: A Gelug Mahāmudrā practised as the union of the sūtra view of emptiness (as in Tsongkhapa) and the tantric clear light; the First Panchen Lama's root text says the Mahāmudrā, Dzogchen, Chöd and Madhyamaka instructions converge in one intent.
summary: The oral 'hearing lineage' of Mahāmudrā and guru yoga that the Gelug traces from Tsongkhapa through Tokden Jampal Gyatso, Baso Chökyi Gyaltsen, Chökyi Dorje and Gyalwa Ensapa to the First Panchen Lama, who set it down in 'The Highway of the Conquerors'.
